title: Motivation
description: The questions behind SRA, from understanding a program's decisions to the purposes and personal convictions that guide its design.
deck: What should we be able to understand about the intelligence we build, and what makes it worth building?
author: Yannick Fontan
intro: When a program solves a puzzle, we can see the result. I also want to understand what made that result possible: what was noticed, which relationships mattered, and why a particular action was chosen. That is a useful place to begin explaining why I am building SRA.

Following this practical question leads to others about meaning, responsibility, and the purposes we give technology. This page follows that path, step by step, toward the personal convictions that give my work its direction.

parts.label: Part I
parts.title: Starting with the work
parts.description: From an interactive puzzle to a reasoning process that people can examine.

steps.title: Start with a small world
paragraphs: An interactive puzzle offers a manageable place to study a difficult problem. There are visible objects, possible actions, and consequences to observe. Even a simple scene requires choices about what to represent and which changes matter.

In SRA, I explore how software can connect those observations to useful actions. A movement might reveal a barrier. A repeated transformation might suggest a rule. Each experiment gives me something concrete to examine, and each unexpected result gives me a reason to look more closely.
steps.consequence: What does the system need to represent before a useful decision becomes possible?

steps.title: Decide what an observation means
paragraphs: A frame contains colors and positions. To work with it, I may need representations of objects, boundaries, roles, or relationships. Those choices shape the kinds of questions the software can address.

Calling something a target already introduces an interpretation. I need to explain what supports that interpretation, how it affects the next action, and what evidence would require changing it. Representation becomes part of the research: I need to understand what a concept means and how it connects to the situation.
steps.consequence: How can a representation stay connected to what can actually be observed and tested?

steps.title: Connect symbols to experience
paragraphs: A symbol becomes useful through its relationships: what it refers to, how it can be used, and what follows from using it. In an interactive environment, those relationships can be examined through action.

For example, if a procedure depends on an object being movable, a controlled attempt can provide relevant evidence. The resulting observation can support that representation or expose a mistake in it. I want those connections to remain accessible to the people designing and evaluating the software.
steps.consequence: If a decision goes wrong, can we follow the path from observation to interpretation to action?

steps.title: Make the decisions inspectable
paragraphs: When an action produces an unexpected result, I want to locate the choices that led to it. Which observations were represented? Which conditions were considered satisfied? Which procedure was selected, and on what basis?

Symbolic reasoning gives me a way to make these elements explicit. Concepts, rules, and intermediate results can become structures people can inspect and discuss. This is why I investigate the approach: I want the design to retain a meaningful connection to human understanding.
steps.consequence: What would show that these explicit structures are useful in practice?

steps.title: Let the experiments constrain the explanation
paragraphs: An explanation needs to remain connected to what happened. If an expected result fails to appear, the implementation, representation, or underlying assumption needs examination. Readability should help us identify the cause.

I therefore want useful records of experiments: starting conditions, actions, observations, and the limits of what can be concluded. SRA and Logos Engine give this investigation a concrete form. The Playground makes parts of it available through games, examples, and explanations of the architecture.
steps.consequence: A game tells us what counts as success. Who makes that choice when we build tools for the wider world?

parts.label: Part II
parts.title: Following the consequences
parts.description: From the choices inside a program to the people and purposes those choices affect.

steps.title: Ask who chooses the objective
paragraphs: A puzzle supplies a relatively clear definition of success. Beyond that setting, the objective itself becomes a design decision. Someone chooses what to measure, which outcomes to pursue, and which costs to accept.

Those choices deserve attention alongside the method used to achieve them. Greater capability makes the purposes assigned to it more consequential. This brings the human designer into view: my responsibility includes the assumptions and priorities I place in the software, and the situations in which I make it available.
steps.consequence: What do people need in order to exercise that responsibility meaningfully?

steps.title: Keep responsibility practical
paragraphs: Responsibility needs workable means. People need enough information to understand a problem, access to investigate it, and the authority to change the relevant decisions. A claim of oversight becomes meaningful through those practical conditions.

This affects how I think about documentation, interfaces, traces, and the distribution of knowledge within a project. I want the people responsible for the software to be able to explain the choices that matter, make limitations visible, and correct their work. This is another reason to care about understandable intelligence.
steps.consequence: Once we can examine a decision, what should guide our judgment of its purpose and consequences?

steps.title: Consider the people affected
paragraphs: Technical measures help me evaluate a tool's accuracy, speed, cost, or reliability. Evaluating its purpose also requires attention to the people whose lives and work it may affect.

I care about their dignity, freedom, vulnerability, and ability to participate in decisions that concern them. A person's worth cannot be read from a performance score. These commitments influence which uses I want to support and what consequences I need to examine. They also shape the way I want to work with others.
steps.consequence: What would make this capability worth building, maintaining, and placing in other people's hands?

steps.title: Build something others can carry forward
paragraphs: Useful knowledge gains reach when other people can understand and develop it. Documentation, teaching, reproducible examples, and collaboration allow work to continue beyond its original author.

I want SRA and Logos Engine to contribute to that kind of capacity. This requires dependable engineering, sustained resources, and people who can become competent contributors in their own right. A result matters, and so does another person's ability to reproduce it, explain it, question it, and use it to create something worthwhile.
steps.consequence: Why do I attach so much importance to understanding, responsibility, and the value of the people this work could serve?

parts.label: Part III
parts.title: Where these questions lead
parts.description: The broader questions behind these choices, and the personal answer through which I understand them.

steps.title: Notice what the work depends on
paragraphs: Following these questions brings me back to what makes my own work possible. I depend on a world I can investigate, a capacity to reason, language learned from others, and knowledge passed across generations. Even an original idea develops from conditions I did not bring into existence myself.

There is a further question here: how should I understand this meeting between a world that can be explored and a mind capable of finding meaning in it? Alongside that question stands another: where do my convictions about human dignity and responsibility find their grounding?
At this point, the inquiry reaches the way I understand my own place in the world.
steps.consequence: What account of existence brings these commitments together for me?

steps.title: Receive existence as a gift
paragraphs: When I bring these questions together, I find a coherent answer in the idea that existence and intelligence have their source in a creative intention. I understand the world as something given, its intelligibility as meaningful, and our capacity to understand as something to receive and develop responsibly.

This is what I mean here by faith in creation: the conviction that the world and human life originate in a Creator. This understanding of creation gives a foundation, for me, to gratitude, inquiry, and responsibility. It also gives depth to the idea that every person has a worth that precedes usefulness.

Seen from this perspective, the project is a way of putting that conviction to work: seeking intelligible structures, examining what I provide in a design, and taking responsibility for its effects. The experiments establish what the software can do; this conviction helps explain why I undertake the work.
steps.consequence: What kind of source do I have in mind, and how does it give a direction to this responsibility?

steps.title: Give that responsibility a direction
paragraphs: For me, the answer takes its fullest form in Jesus Christ. John's Gospel presents him as the Logos, the Word through whom creation comes into being and who enters human life. I understand the source of reason and meaning as personal. In his life and Cross, I find a connection between truth and love, between power and service, and between knowing and caring.

Grace gives another part of the answer: a worth received before achievement, from which good work can grow. This is the Christian faith in which the threads of this reflection meet for me. It gives personal meaning to the dignity, responsibility, and service discussed along the way. The name Logos Engine acknowledges that connection; its design and consequences remain a human responsibility.

One hope that follows is to see more Christians develop real competence in the field of intelligence, make symbolic methods their own, and contribute through useful tools, teaching, and lasting institutions. I want this capacity to be shared widely, in collaboration with people working for the common good. That is how I hope to honor Christ through what I build.
steps.consequence: Build intelligence that people can understand and take responsibility for, develop the capability to make it useful, and pass that knowledge on in a spirit of service.

closing.title: Continue with the project
closing.text: The pages that follow explore how these intentions take shape in a method, an architecture, and experiments you can examine for yourself.
